agent-regression.title: Agent Regression
agent-regression.text:
Agent release decisions that only check the final answer miss wrong tools, repeated side effects and invented evidence.
Caught 128/128 injected faults across 8 fault types on a deterministic fixture agent; 21/21 baseline contracts pass.
A correct answer is insufficient when the agent used the wrong tool, repeated an effect, or invented its evidence. This suite grades the visible output and execution trace against independent arithmetic labels, then compares complete runs before making a release decision.
The supplied candidate deliberately breaks add-positive. Exit status 1 is the expected result for that comparison. Comparing the baseline to itself exits 0. Missing cases block the gate instead of disappearing from the denominator.
To generate and grade the local fixture:
The fixture is a deterministic arithmetic agent with four allowlisted tools. It makes no model calls. Its 21 labeled cases and eight named executable faults exercise the harness; they are not a measurement of LLM reasoning.
A statistical comparison binds the labeled dataset, baseline/candidate versions, replay hashes, declared slices, minimum sample sizes and critical cases:
The supplied 240-case synthetic run recorded 213 baseline successes and 232 candidate successes. A separately versioned candidate with a critical-case fault is blocked. Exact McNemar/binomial tails and Holm correction test deterioration; conservative simultaneous bounds support the noninferiority check. Bootstrap intervals are descriptive and do not authorize release by themselves.
These are fixed-sample calculations over independent case pairs. Repeated peeking, clustered cases and selecting slices after seeing outcomes require different inference. The release mathematics states the assumptions and alpha allocation.
Every successful record has a typed answer, the selected tool, a call ID and the actual observable tool event. Unknown fields, duplicate executions, forged evidence, malformed errors and unbounded input fail validation. Imported traces are checked for internal consistency; the file format does not attest that another system actually executed them.
Fault reports distinguish attempted, unchanged, ineligible and detected injections. Existing baseline failures cannot increase the mutation score. The recorded fixture run passed 21/21 baseline contracts, detected 128/128 eligible named faults and passed 48/48 paired metamorphic cases. The complete suite contains 44 tests.
The replay format and validator findings explain the edge cases. Fault-probe results preserve selected source-fault probes without presenting them as whole-project mutation coverage.
Python 3.11+ is sufficient. Running the gates covers interpretation; sharing a suite covers release files. A different tool environment needs its own independent oracle and labels before these checks can grade it.

capability-guard.title: Capability Guard
capability-guard.text:
An LLM agent can be talked into calling tools it should not; a valid credential can still be unusable.
HMAC-signed, attenuable capabilities with quotas, revocation and replay protection; 17 adversarial tests.
An authentic credential can still be unusable. Its MAC may verify after its quota is exhausted or its issuer key is revoked. The distinction is the main interface in this library:
The trusted host issues HMAC-SHA256 capabilities for three fictional note operations. An agent can propose a typed request; it cannot grant itself a scope by putting instructions in the text. Issuance, attenuation, rotation, and revocation stay outside the tool allowlist.
Python 3.11+ and its standard library are sufficient.
The demo appends 24 bytes, rejects a repeated nonce, and rejects an ungranted resource. Keys, bearer credentials, and the database are temporary. The saved receipt contains no key or bearer token.
attenuate() is issuer-controlled reissuance. Children may narrow scope, resources, lifetime, and budgets. Every child invocation charges all ancestors, so splitting a grant into children cannot multiply its quota. A child also depends on every ancestor and key remaining active.
The nonce, quota updates, and effect share one SQLite transaction. A request waiting behind a write lock sees a revocation committed before it proceeds. Expiry is reread after the wait.
Start with credential and quota rules, then the transaction boundary. The authorization regressions and replay trials record 17 passing contracts and the exercised concurrency cases.
The host process, keys, clock, SQLite store, and filesystem are trusted. HMAC uses a shared secret, not public-key signatures. The subject denotes a host context, not a human login. A stolen bearer can spend its remaining rights. Arbitrary code execution or direct database edits bypass this library; logical tool limits are not an OS sandbox. Only this database's local effects participate in the transaction. Never print or commit issuer keys, bearer credentials, or private database contents.

chronofeature.title: Chronofeature
chronofeature.text:
A purchase happened at time 10 but was first observed at time 15. A decision at time 12 must not use it. A decision at time 20 may.
Event time alone cannot answer that question. Chronofeature keeps observation time and ingestion generation alongside each immutable event revision, then applies all three cutoffs before building a feature.
The target stays outside feature queries. source_generation= can reproduce a historical ingestion snapshot after backfills. Previously published versions remain immutable.
SQLite resolves visible revisions with an indexed ASOF query. Integer prefix sums and binary-search cutoffs compute count, sum, mean, and latest value across configured windows. The point-in-time rules define exact boundaries and complexity. Availability timestamps are source declarations; the engine cannot detect a dishonest source clock.
Serving returns the materialization time, source generation, and specification hash. It does not recompute aggregates at each request. A cached window expires at the earlier relevant TTL or membership boundary; once an included event falls out of the window, its old sum cannot remain available merely because the latest event is fresh.
New arrivals may require refreshing a still-unexpired snapshot. Publishing a new version writes all entity rows, metadata, and the active pointer in one transaction. Replaying an older version cannot move that pointer backward. A changed definition needs a new (name, version) specification identity.
The recorded run checks 120 independent scan comparisons plus 18 generation, target-isolation, atomicity, replay, and expiry cases: 138/138 invariants. Its 112 initial revisions include corrections and tombstones, followed by backfills. The tests also run seeds 23 and 101. No model accuracy or serving-throughput result is inferred from these checks.
Feature flow, temporal regressions, and parity runs cover the implementation. The store uses integer-valued signals and local SQLite transactions. Distributed cache invalidation, streaming watermarks, and automatic refresh are not implemented.

constrained-generation.title: Constrained Generation
constrained-generation.text:
MOVE N 3;STOP parses, but it walks off a 5x5 board when the robot starts in the center. STOP is safe and well formed, but it does not carry out an instruction to move east. This project keeps those failures separate while comparing unconstrained decoding, grammar masks, and state-aware masks.
The language is deliberately small:
Spacing is literal, as in MOVE E 2;PICK a;STOP. The interpreter checks position, item ownership, and a six-cell movement budget. Programs cannot invoke Python, a shell, or external tools.
Python 3.11+ is sufficient for the replay experiments. The synthetic policy assigns preferences to known candidate strings; it is not a language model. Every approach sees the same scores, including the reference completion. Reports retain syntax validity, executability, final state, action-aware instruction success, and exhausted budgets.
The recorded beam run illustrates a search-objective problem:
A short STOP can outrank a longer correct answer under raw sequence likelihood. The search does not add an undisclosed length bonus to hide that result. The experiment note records candidate expansions, policy calls, and the exact setup.
The compiled machine carries grammar position, completed-command count, robot state, and movement budget. A shared vocabulary trie avoids checking every token against every full prefix. Semantic masking uses the initial state and legal actions; it never reads the expected program or goal. Accepted prefixes have executable continuations, but a token cap can still end a run before completion.
Beam scores include EOS and use the original conditional log probabilities, without renormalizing after masking. Completed hypotheses are retained separately. Narrow beams are not guaranteed to recover the globally most likely program.
Known standalone ByteLevel decoders use compiled masks. Other tokenizers use a full-suffix reference path; --force-reference makes that comparison explicit. Sparse vocabulary IDs and model-output bounds are checked. Inherited forced-EOS and minimum-length settings cannot override the mask. Loading is local-only, and the scorer recomputes prefixes rather than claiming KV-cache acceleration.
Random tiny-checkpoint integration tests have run. No useful pretrained-model score is supplied.
Run python -m unittest discover -s tests -v. With the optional ML dependencies installed, use RUN_ML_SMOKE=1 to include the local-checkpoint tests. For wheel and formatting checks, run python devtools/check_decoder.py --require-lint --wheel.
The state map, trial protocol, and check record describe the rest of the evidence. Historical trace paths refer to the layout used when those runs were recorded.

count-lineages.title: Count Lineages, Not Checkpoints
count-lineages.text:
Code, results and paper source for Count Lineages, Not Checkpoints: LLMs Are Not Independent Test-Takers.
Item-level analyses of LLM benchmarks (item response models, label-error screens, differential item functioning) treat every evaluated model as an independent respondent. Most leaderboard entries share a base model with many others. This repository measures what that does to uncertainty and provides a tool to account for it.
Paper: rewrite/main.pdf. It has not been peer reviewed; see Status and limitations.
The numbers are the ones in the abstract. Every number in the paper is generated from the stored result files; Check the numbers shows how to regenerate them.
It prints the archive panel's composition and the ARC screening audit:
pip install -e '.[test]' && python -m pytest -q inside modelkin/ runs its 14 tests.
The paper's tables and in-text numbers are built from the stored result files in pilot_neff/. With NumPy and SciPy installed (the modelkin install above brings both):
make_tables.py also rewrites pilot_neff/validation.json, whose correlations can differ in the last floating-point digits on another NumPy build. This re-runs the table step only. The simulations, bootstraps, audits and metadata fetches behind the stored result files take longer and some need network access; the next section covers them.
rewrite/README.md lists the commands in order. Three inputs are fetched by the scripts and are not stored here:
item-level responses for the newer leaderboard, from the RouterEval release
(leaderboard_score.zip, read only through pilot_neff/safe_pickle.py);
GSM8K-Platinum and MMLU-Redux error annotations;
live repository metadata from Hugging Face (snapshots of what was retrieved on
15 November 2026 are stored in pilot_neff/).
Run the scripts from inside pilot_neff/. Several of them are plain scripts that execute on import, so run them, do not import them.
Single-author work that has not been peer reviewed or checked by an independent human
reviewer. rewrite/README.md records its review history.
No item-level responses for 2025-26 models were found publicly at scale; the newest panel
ends in March 2025.
The label-error and DIF re-audits re-run published procedures without reproducing the
original pipelines.
Family labels come from Hugging Face metadata retrieved on 15 November 2026. Re-fetching can
change them if repositories have been edited or deleted since.
Code: MIT (see LICENSE). Data: see evalens_release_package/DATA_SOURCES.md and the licence files next to it; the benchmark question text in data/cache/ remains under its upstream licences.

drift-sentinel.title: Drift Sentinel
drift-sentinel.text:
Twenty-four stationary trajectories produced no alert openings in the saved run. Their approximate 95% interval still reaches 0.138. That gap matters: a quiet small experiment does not establish zero false-alert risk.
The same experiment detected all 24 feature-mean shifts and all 24 classification-loss increases, with median delays of 255 and 270 request indices. Those are separate signals. A changed input mean says something about incoming data; worse predictions require joined outcomes.
The trajectory record keeps the seeds, sample counts, stream fingerprints, censoring and per-scenario results. Each trajectory has 2,048 predictions, independent historical calibration and labels delayed by 0 to 31 indices. Its thresholds were not tuned on those evaluation seeds. The change-trajectory notes give the full setup and limits.
A label can precede or follow its prediction. Their request ID binds the pair, and the join computes classification error once. An unlabeled prediction contributes its feature value but no invented quality result. Identical duplicates are idempotent; conflicting duplicates and exhausted pending-state capacity fail explicitly.
Each metric/segment gets a fixed part of the monitoring epoch's alpha budget. Look j spends that part times 6/(pi² j²). The two-sample boundary includes the finite historical reference's uncertainty. Opening requires consecutive positive looks; resolution uses a narrower exit band, followed by cooldown. None of those transitions resets the spending clock.
The false-opening bound assumes independent stationary bounded observations, an independent historical cohort, and noninformative label arrival. It is unconditional over reference and future sampling. It does not hold conditionally for every realized reference. Informative missing labels change the population represented by observed quality.
This monitor tracks mean shifts. A variance change with the same mean may remain invisible. It is also in-memory: a fresh instance starts another epoch, so repeated restarts need a higher-level error budget. The demo's global quality alert opens at index 400 and resolves at 718; segment recovery can take longer.
Python 3.11 or later is sufficient; the runtime has no external dependencies.
The 14 tests include 54 independently enumerated small-sample null checks, alpha-budget summability, delayed joins, hysteresis/cooldown and finite text exports.
src/drift_sentinel/monitor.py contains the joins, channels and alert state.
monitoring/default.json records the default settings.
measurements/ holds JSON and Prometheus output from executed runs.
Spending and delay derives the statistical assumptions.
Observation path and null/lifecycle checks locate the state transitions and tests.

eventflow.title: Eventflow
eventflow.text:
A late value changes an already published window. Replaying that source record leaves the corrected result alone. The small stream in streams/stream.jsonl makes both behaviors visible:
These steps use lag 2 and allowed lateness 5. Online features and inference telemetry need this sort of policy whenever source time, arrival order and retries disagree.
The first command commits ten unique records and sees one duplicate. The second sees eleven duplicates and leaves checkpoint/sink state unchanged. Each source input is its own transaction, so a failed input does not undo the earlier committed prefix.
A source identity is (partition, offset). Offsets may have gaps or arrive out of numeric order. The processor records the exact identity and payload fingerprint; reusing an identity with different content raises a conflict.
Windows are half-open and aligned to slide. Setting slide equal to window size produces tumbling windows; smaller slides overlap. One event can be closed out of an older sliding window while still contributing to a newer one.
The watermark is the minimum progress across all configured partitions, less the allowed out-of-orderness. An unseen or stalled partition holds it back. advance records are explicit source progress assertions, not a guessed idle-partition timeout. A window closes inclusively at end + allowed_lateness.
Source identities, progress, aggregate state, sink changes and checkpoint metadata commit together. A crash before commit rolls them back; a crash after commit is handled by replay deduplication. The guarantee ends at the local SQLite database. A remote broker or consumer needs its own acknowledgement and idempotency protocol.
The 17 tests include a crash during a late sink revision, atomic capacity failures and maximal-timestamp draining. The saved [evaluation passed 30/30 scenarios across window/lateness policies, both commit boundaries and twelve seeded out-of-order streams. Its oracle retains individual contributions and recomputes sums independently; a second consumer rebuilds the sink from duplicate-delivered changelog entries.
State has finite limits. Closed active windows are evicted, while source identities and final sink rows remain until the application's retention boundary. Reaching a configured capacity rolls back the current input rather than silently losing replay identity. The watermark contract lists those bounds and the storage assumptions.
Event to sink maps the components; window histories records the workloads. Run python dev/check_recovery.py --require-lint --wheel for the full installation check.

hard-negative-retrieval.title: Hard-negative retrieval
hard-negative-retrieval.text:
Approximate indexes trade recall for speed, and perfect candidate recall still does not make a ranking correct.
Index recall@5 vs exhaustive MaxSim rises from 0.74 (1 probe, 16 candidates) to 1.00 (8 probes, 96 candidates).
Probing every index cluster reproduces the exhaustive ranking. That does not make the ranking correct.
On the recorded 96-document corpus, exhaustive MaxSim places the relevant document first for 74/128 queries: 64/64 alias questions and 10/64 relation-binding questions. The latter swap roles while keeping the same token multiset. Non-contextual token vectors cannot distinguish those documents, even with perfect candidate recall.
Per-query index results keep relevance separate from agreement with the scoring oracle. Late-interaction results explain the difficult slice and measured work.
Python 3.11+ is sufficient for the training and index code. There are no required third-party packages.
The coarse partition uses spherical k-means++. Candidates are reranked by the same normalized-token MaxSim function as exhaustive search. Saved indexes bind the corpus and both raw and normalized encoder state. Loading rejects stale bindings, missing or duplicate postings, nonfinite centroids, and inconsistent assignments.
The dual encoder learns separate mean-pooled token tables with InfoNCE and SGD. Hard mining begins with lexical negatives and then uses model rankings; the random-negative ablation excludes the same known positives and preserves update order. Development and test labels do not enter training.
This workload gives no evidence that hard negatives outperform random negatives. It shares products, intents, aliases, and corpus text across query-template splits. The reference data and results retain that narrower interpretation.
Scoring and partition rules cover complexity and artifact validation. Encoder/index flow describes component boundaries. Numerical checks records regressions, and retrieval runs lists comparison commands.
Text is bounded to 5,000 characters and 128 retained tokens; the corpus supports at most 1,000 documents. Training and query work have explicit limits. Unknown-only learned queries return no hits. These token vectors are neither contextual transformer outputs nor parameters trained with a MaxSim objective. The optional sentence-transformers adapter is separate and unmeasured here. Sharing a new corpus or index requires the identities and split information described in the index release notes.

incremental-lakehouse.title: Incremental lakehouse
incremental-lakehouse.text:
A batch is staged before it is published. That separation lets ingestion resume after a partial write without exposing half-updated analytical tables.
The publish transaction advances source offsets, selects current rows, maintains derived views, records quarantine, and moves the batch checkpoint together. A failed publish leaves the staged input available for retry. Readers keep seeing the previous committed snapshot.
The same path is available through the Python API:
stage stores the immutable payload and durable chunk cursor. recover(batch_id) finishes incomplete staging and publishes. Reusing a batch ID with different content fails. Exact published replays return the stored report.
Offsets are contiguous per source/partition. An exact replay is ignored; a conflicting payload at the same offset or a gap rejects the batch. Cursor progress is separate from row version: a late valid event can consume an offset while leaving the winning row unchanged.
Winner ordering is (event_time, source, partition, offset). Deletes retain tombstones, so an older backfill cannot resurrect a deleted key. This is a declared conflict policy; a source needing another policy must change the contract explicitly.
Row and quality errors enter quarantine and consume their offset. Unknown tables and incompatible schema changes abort publication. Evolution permits additive nullable/defaulted fields, relaxed nullability, and integer-to-float widening. Source rows are normalized through their declared schema before applying the current one.
Derived filters and grouped sum/count models consume coalesced old/new key contributions. Group transfers, refunds, and deletes subtract the old contribution and add the new one. An unchanged view does not invent a new content generation or invalidate descendants. The CDC and view rules specify rational accumulation, schema checks, lineage, and complexity.
The seed-17 run consumes 120 unique events in 12 published batches: 53/53 invariants, seven quarantines, 11 exact duplicates, and 26 older valid versions ignored. Every batch is compared with an independent full-history rebuild. These are controlled correctness results, not throughput measurements.
Publication flow, recovery cases, and change-stream runs describe the boundaries exercised by tests. Batches, retained offsets/keys, schema changes, and DAG nodes have explicit caps. SQLite serializes writers; external source acknowledgements do not join its transaction. No distributed scheduler, object-store connector, retention service, or remote source is included.

model-ledger.title: Model Ledger
model-ledger.text:
Two release jobs can both read staging revision zero. Only one should publish revision one. Model Ledger makes that decision with a compare-and-swap transaction and records the winning release in a hash-chained audit log.
Use a fresh registry directory for this example. Both expected-zero arguments require a new name or environment. For an existing registry, read its current head/revision before requesting a change. Dataset and configuration manifests can be supplied as parents of a model manifest, preserving the release's lineage.
A manifest names immutable bytes by SHA256. Promotion walks its transitive lineage and verifies the reachable bytes before changing an environment reference. Rollback creates another release revision pointing to an earlier target; it does not rewrite old records. If retention has already collected those bytes, rollback fails until the same content is uploaded again.
The ingest lease closes the gap between uploading bytes and attaching them to a manifest. Collection uses the same writer lock as promotion and lease renewal, so a successful active release cannot become a dangling reference through that race. Files are quarantined before collection commits, allowing recovery to distinguish an interrupted transaction from completed deletion.
This is a local filesystem/SQLite registry. It verifies byte identity and release metadata; it does not authenticate tenants or establish that a model's training data is truthful. The application owns the registry directory and its database.
Python 3.11 or later is enough; there are no runtime dependencies.
The CLI creates temporary registries, performs the operations, and exports JSON. The recorded evaluation contains eight local integrity/lifecycle checks and a four-promoter race with one winner. The 17-test suite also exits subprocesses at publication and collection boundaries, checks quarantine restoration, and races promotion against collection. Its weight fixtures are ordinary bytes, not trained checkpoints.
Promotion rehashes all reachable lineage bytes while holding the writer lock. That cost is deliberate and limits concurrency for large artifacts. Uploads are capped at 256 MiB, and lineage traversal has a 10,000-manifest bound. File fsync and SQLite FULL synchronization are used; process-exit experiments do not establish behavior under every power or storage failure.
Artifact paths maps the components. For a full local build check, use python tools/check_registry.py --require-lint --wheel; sharing the ledger explains the release files to retain.

model-router.title: Model Router
model-router.text:
At a budget of 180 configured units, the recorded 36-case arithmetic fixture gives this result:
Those responses and costs are simulated. The logistic predictor and calibration are actually fitted, but the table is not a provider benchmark or a monetary-savings claim. Across five arrival orders, the frozen learned policy solved 24 to 27 cases at budget 180. At budget 40 it solved 5 to 8, while fixed-small solved 8 to 12. The learned policy does not win every regime.
The batch router receives an expression's syntax features and pre-dispatch cost quotes. It cannot read the candidate outputs or the arithmetic answer. Expression structures are split into 108 training, 36 calibration, and 36 test records. Training fits a small-model success predictor; calibration fits probabilities and chooses a threshold under an explicit budget. Test labels enter evaluation only.
Before any recorded response is consumed, the selected quote must fit the remaining budget. Otherwise the policy chooses an affordable alternative or abstains. The exact batch oracle sees labels offline, buys the cheapest correct cases, and supplies an upper bound; it is not available to routing.
Python 3.11+ and the standard library are enough.
Generate and train a new fixture with generate and train. The versioned router records training/calibration hashes, structural group sets, and the threshold-selection budget. Loading an older schema-1 artifact fails rather than guessing its missing budget. The evaluator rejects declared train/test overlap.
Imported JSONL can instead contain RECORDED responses with exact model identity and timezone-qualified capture time. Keep latency_ms null unless measured. Integer cost_units express the chosen budget policy, not a currency conversion. Imports are bounded to 33,554,432 characters with per-line checks; router artifacts are capped at 1,048,576 characters. Duplicate JSON fields and nonfinite numbers are rejected. See the record format and leakage rules.
The logged-bandit subsystem evaluates stateless per-request policies under individual cost caps. It does not apply one-step importance weights to the budget-coupled batch allocator.
Only the chosen action's outcome reaches the estimator. IPS, SNIPS, and cross-fitted doubly robust estimates are compared with full-information synthetic truth outside estimation. The stored adaptive-policy run has truth 0.477333, IPS 0.470392, SNIPS 0.473689, DR 0.475168, and effective sample size 1,305.59. Unsupported target actions yield no estimate; low evidence makes the exported result unusable. Confidence intervals have the assumptions stated in the estimator derivation, not an unrestricted repeated-peeking guarantee.
Run python -m unittest discover -s test -v, then python tools/check_routing.py --require-lint --wheel for repository checks. Routing regressions, offline evaluation instructions, and the check ledger retain the evidence and its limits. No API collection or live model dispatch is performed here.

pixel-to-program.title: Pixel to Program
pixel-to-program.text:
The image above is the renderer's ground truth, not a model prediction. The learning task goes in the other direction: read the 32x32 image, produce a program, execute it, and compare the reconstructed scene. A legal output can still draw the wrong shapes, which is why parsing and reconstruction have separate scores.
These commands use only Python 3.11+ and the standard library. demo writes SVG, binary PPM, and a known program. The default evaluate checks 36 codec/renderer roundtrips and a blank baseline. It explicitly marks learned-model evaluation false.
The language has rectangles and ellipses in red, blue, or green, bounded integer coordinates, and at most four shapes. Later shapes cover earlier ones. Input images use the project's strict 32x32 binary PPM format; arbitrary SVG input is not accepted.
Training sees red/blue rectangles and red/green ellipses. Development introduces green rectangles; test introduces blue ellipses. A designated held-out primitive must remain visibly responsible for at least half its foreground. Global raster/program hashes prevent split duplicates, and manifest loading verifies the image against its program. This controls one compositional question, not natural-image recognition.
train-system uses spatial patches, learned row/column positions, a visual Transformer encoder, and a causal program decoder with cross attention. --architecture cnn_gru selects the comparator under the same optimizer, data order, loss, and search interfaces. The two models are not parameter matched, and their regularization differs.
Training uses AdamW, clipping, warmup/cosine scheduling, optional label smoothing, and token-weighted development NLL. Latest resume state and best-development inference weights share one atomic checkpoint. Resume restores optimizer/schedule progress, Python/Torch RNG, and dataset/configuration identity. An executed CPU regression compares uninterrupted and resumed weights with dropout enabled; GPU determinism is not claimed.
Inference encodes the image once, batches beam prefixes, and keeps original model likelihood after grammar filtering. Completed hypotheses are archived. Width one remains actual greedy decoding. Grammar masks track field types, shape count, geometry bounds, and EOS placement; they do not establish that a scene matches the input.
The paired short run used 16 training, four development, and four test scenes, with two seeds and two epochs per architecture. Both models produced 8/8 grammar-valid constrained greedy outputs, but 0/8 exact raster matches. The denominator counts four scenes across two seeds, not eight distinct scenes. Transformer development NLL was worse in that run. The recorded experiment gives parameter counts and the full ablation conditions.
Use validity, exact raster match, foreground IoU, RGB error, and primitive extraction together. Wrong colors can leave foreground IoU unchanged. Invalid predictions keep their raw token IDs and errors; the code never replaces them with ground-truth programs. The legacy train/evaluate-model commands remain available for the original CNN/GRU baseline.
src/pixel_to_program/scene.py and data.py: scene language, rendering, visibility and split validation.
src/pixel_to_program/attention_model.py, attention_training.py, and attention_inference.py: neural path and resumable optimization.
src/pixel_to_program/search.py: likelihood search and completion handling.
gallery/: source scene and recorded outputs.
reference/attention-and-search.md: equations, state, complexity, and checkpoint behavior.
tools/probe_rendering_contract.py: selected regressions checked in temporary copies.
Run RUN_ML_SMOKE=1 PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v with Torch installed. python tools/check_vision.py --require-lint --wheel checks packaging as well. Rendering defects, training notes, and the check history document the evidence. No pretrained VLM or useful held-out reconstruction score is supplied.

plandesk.title: PlanDesk
plandesk.text:
Retirement-plan limits change every year, and an assistant that answers from memory or from the wrong year's document gives confident wrong numbers.
97.1% correct on 35 answerable questions, 7/7 out-of-scope questions refused, every answer backed by a quote that is checked against the source. Closed book: 94.3% with no checkable source, and 3 of 7 out-of-scope questions answered anyway.
Ask a question about U.S. retirement-plan rules. PlanDesk searches IRS Publications 590-A, 590-B and 560 (2024 and 2025 editions), answers with a real LLM, and shows the exact sentence each answer came from. If the publications don't say, it refuses.
42 hand-written questions: 35 answerable (contribution limits, a year trap where both editions repeat the same sentence with different numbers, next-year amounts, distribution rules) and 7 the publications can't answer (2028 and 2030 limits, HSA and FSA limits, state tax, fund picks, a company's match formula).
Full per-category table and every miss: evals/REPORT.md.
Check these numbers without an API key: uv sync && uv run python scripts/report.py rebuilds evals/REPORT.md from the committed runs in evals/results/, and uv run pytest re-scores them against the release gate.
What the numbers say, including the unflattering parts
Retrieval is the big win. But not for raw accuracy. Closed book scored 94.3% because the model already knows most 2024 and 2025 limits. The difference is trust: closed book answered 3 of the 7 questions the publications don't cover (HSA, FSA, California tax) with no source to check, and its 2 misses were confident and wrong, such as telling a 55-year-old that the 2025 IRA limit is $7,000 when Pub. 590-A says $8,000. With retrieval, every answer comes with a quote you can open, and out-of-scope questions are refused.
The smaller model refuses too often. gpt-5.4-nano with the same pipeline got 88.6%: all 4 misses were refusals, two of them from the guard rejecting quotes that weren't verbatim. It never gave a wrong number, which is the failure mode the guard is designed to trade for.
The year filter did not change accuracy on this set. Naive RAG, with both editions in context, scored the same as the full pipeline. The model reads "for 2024" vs "for 2025" correctly once the passage is in front of it. A harder test would need questions where the year is implied rather than stated.
"Supported" is stricter than "correct". For the age-50 total deferral question the model correctly added $23,500 + $7,500 = $31,000, but no single cited sentence states $31,000, so it counts as correct but not supported. That is the right call for an audit trail: arithmetic the user can't trace to a sentence should be flagged.
One refusal was a model error. On the first-home question the model had the right quote ($10,000) and still refused.
Small set, written by me. 42 questions is enough to catch regressions, not to claim general accuracy. The questions were written while building the system, so this is not a held-out benchmark.
Bugs the eval caught during development
The model sometimes wrapped citation IDs in brackets ([560-2025-p10-c2]). Normalizing the IDs fixed it, and a test now covers it.
One expected answer was wrong: I had expected "12 months" for the IRA rollover frequency, but the publication says "1-year period". The label was corrected to accept the source's wording.
Embeddings for the corpus are built on first use and cached in data/embeddings.npy (about 11 MB, not committed).
uv run pytest needs no API key. It tests chunking, matching, retrieval with year filters, quote verification and scoring, then re-scores every committed run in evals/results/ and fails if the full pipeline drops below 90% accuracy or misses any refusal.
Corpus freshness: watch irs.gov for new editions and rebuild; record the edition date in every citation.
Printed page numbers: citations use PDF page numbers today; map them to printed pages.
Arithmetic: route sums (like base limit + catch-up) through a calculator tool so the derivation is shown and checkable.
Harder eval: implied-year questions, multi-hop rules, and a held-out set written by someone else.
Cost tracking: reports carry raw token counts; add current per-token prices to PRICES in answer.py for dollar estimates.
IRS publications are U.S. government works in the public domain. Code is MIT. Not tax, legal or investment advice.

query-forge.title: Query Forge
query-forge.text:
Start with a query, then inspect the work its plan actually performs:
The saved plan comparison returns the same two groups with both executors. The reference checks 100,644 nested-loop pairs. The optimized plan builds 31 hash rows and performs 805 probes. Projection pushdown materializes 2,568 cells instead of 5,132. Predicate applications increase from 99 to 1,204 because the filters run earlier; these counters are different kinds of work, not a latency ratio.
Python 3.11+ and its standard library are sufficient. --reference selects the original join order and nested loops; --batch-size controls operator batches. The CLI uses a seeded catalog, while Engine and Table accept other typed input snapshots. SQL proposed by an agent follows the same parser and binder as any other input.
The grammar covers selected columns or unqualified *, aliases, inner equijoins, comparisons, NULL predicates, boolean expressions, five aggregates, grouping, and LIMIT. It excludes ordering, outer joins, subqueries, DDL/DML, arbitrary functions, and text/numeric affinity coercion. Unsupported SQL fails instead of being delegated to SQLite or Python evaluation.
NULL comparisons yield UNKNOWN; filters keep TRUE only. Hash buckets exclude NULL keys and retain duplicate cross products. NULL grouping keys form one group. Empty global aggregates return one row with COUNT zero and other results NULL; grouped empty input returns no rows.
Join order can change both floating rounding and intermediate integer overflow. SUM/AVG therefore use exact accumulators with conservative order-stability certificates. INTEGER SUM bounds positive and negative subtotals separately. Floating aggregation requires a common binary grid whose scaled absolute subtotal fits 53 bits and whose absolute-value bound remains finite.
1e16,-1e16,1 and some otherwise valid SQLite decimal sequences are rejected consistently by both plans. The certificate is intentionally narrower than arbitrary finite SQL aggregation. It prevents a join rewrite from silently changing the answer; the SQL and numeric contract derives the rule.
LIMIT without ORDER BY also has no specified row choice. Differential checks enforce cardinality and duplicate-aware membership in the unlimited SQLite result rather than assuming its physical ordering.
The plan-work record includes 75 seeded differential queries, with catalog analysis reported separately. The conformance findings cover randomized checks and cancellation regressions. Operators exchange Python batches, not native SIMD vectors. Hash joins keep a build side in memory; there is no spill, index, distributed backend, or host resource sandbox.

quorum-lab.title: Quorum Lab
quorum-lab.text:
A minority leader accepts a write, then the network heals. That write must not appear in the committed history merely because it was accepted locally. The seed-7 history follows this case through a replacement election, crash/restart, suffix repair, and final convergence.
raft.Node.Propose reports acceptance, not commitment. The committed prefix is a separate observation through Status or Applied. This distinction matters for any replicated control plane that coordinates model versions, routing rules, or worker assignments.
An actual Go 1.23+ SDK is required; the recorded run used Go 1.25.1. There are no external modules.
The binary and go run use the same demo|evaluate [--output PATH] interface. Failed scenarios exit 1; invalid CLI/output failures exit 2. make test GO=/path/to/real/go also accepts an explicit SDK path.
Elections use randomized deadlines and last-term/last-index freshness. A leader writes a current-term no-op, replicates bounded batches, and commits only a current-term entry with majority evidence. Follower commit is bounded by the prefix verified in that append; a long local tail is not proof that the leader verified it. Per-peer sequence handling prevents old failures from undoing newer replication progress.
Nodes have one serialized owner. Static three- and five-member identities are persisted and cannot be replaced through a restart. MemoryStore is the simulator's crash-surviving model. FileStore actually writes a temporary whole-state file, syncs it, renames it, and syncs the directory. Checksums detect corruption; they do not authenticate a malicious rewrite. One process owns each file, with no cross-process file lock.
The recorded exploration covers seeds 1-12 for each cluster size: 24 scenarios of 360 ticks, with partitions, 0-15% phase-specific loss, reordering, and restart. All 24 completed their expected commands, while no minority-only command committed. The partition histories retain the manifest hash, 52,780 safety observations, and transport counts. A safety observation is not a unique explored state, and the retained trace prefix is not a complete event log.
Membership changes, snapshots, read-index/linearizable reads, real RPC, client deduplication, and external application transactions are outside this implementation. File tests exercise sync/rename/recovery but do not emulate power loss. Log, message, command, and tick budgets fail explicitly rather than silently dropping state. The persistence and commit rules define those limits; protocol regressions describe the failures the tests guard against.

resilient-agent-runtime.title: Resilient agent runtime
resilient-agent-runtime.text:
When an agent crashes between a side effect and its acknowledgement, a naive retry runs the effect twice.
Transactional outbox/inbox with payload-bound deduplication passes 12/12 defined failure cases.
The receiver commits a credit. The sender dies before recording the acknowledgement. On restart, should the command run again?
This implementation redelivers the same message. The receiver checks its retained inbox key and payload, then returns a duplicate receipt without adding another credit. Sender and receiver use separate SQLite databases; there is no transaction spanning them.
The last row matters: a dead letter does not prove that no effect occurred.
The recorded replay shows both durable stores before and after recovery. The protocol experiment passed 12/12 defined cases, including eight concurrent deliveries, an admission race, payload conflict, outage/restart, and an actual child-process exit after receiver commit. This is an invariant count, not an availability percentage.
Workflow completion means the intent is durable, not that the receiver has applied it. Admission reserves future enqueue slots when a plan is submitted. The default backlog limit is 128 reserved or undelivered messages; delivery attempts are capped at five. Dead letters retain capacity until reconciliation. Message identity includes a persistent sender namespace, workflow, and action; a changed payload cannot reuse an inbox key.
A lease epoch fences sender queue updates. It cannot retract a receiver transaction. Cancellation stops uncommitted workflow actions, while already committed outbox intents remain deliverable. The delivered result flag means the sender accepted an ACK; False leaves the receiver outcome potentially uncertain.
The base Runtime also supports fictional credits entirely within one database. Its effect, ledger, checkpoint, and event share a transaction; attempts are persisted separately. Final commit gates check cancellation, deadlines, and lease ownership. Invocation deadlines are cooperative and cannot kill a stuck Python hook.
The recorded local evaluation passes 31/31 scenarios. The complete suite contains 64 tests, including separate connections, real concurrent deliveries, and abrupt process exits.
Commit boundaries, failure regressions, fault scenarios, and ACK-gap results separate the local and two-store guarantees. The transport is an in-process adapter between real durable files. Inbox retention, stable message identity, continued scheduling, and receiver availability are assumptions.

servegate.title: ServeGate
servegate.text:
A gateway that sits in front of a model server, written in Go with only the standard library. It provides deadline-aware microbatching, fair per-tenant admission, cancellation and circuit breaking. The backend is deterministic CPU work, so the results describe the queue and the batching, not model throughput.
Start the gateway, submit a request, then inspect what waited before the backend ran:
From another terminal:
X-Timeout-Ms can shorten the request budget. X-Tenant-ID is a caller-supplied label in this lab; an authenticated service would derive that identity before admission. The default backend performs deterministic SHA-256 CPU work. It gives the scheduler observable work without making a model-throughput claim.
One scheduler goroutine owns the tenant queues. Admission retains a global permit until the request has actually left the scheduler/backend, including after a client disconnects. Each tenant has an outstanding-request limit, tenants take turns round robin, and each tenant's queue uses earliest deadline first.
A batch flushes at its size limit, collection-window expiry, an imminent deadline, or drain. Cancellation of one member leaves other members running; cancellation of every member cancels the cooperative batch context. Late backend results are rejected. An arbitrary stuck Go function still needs to return before its worker can be reused.
Retries require both operator RetrySafe=true and the adapter's transient-error classification. The request cannot enable retries. Breaker permits carry generations so an old completion cannot close a newer open circuit. Closing the gateway rejects new admission, drains accepted work, and cancels cooperative workers when its close deadline expires.
Defaults are batch size eight, two workers, 128 outstanding requests globally, 32 per tenant, 16 active tenant labels, and a 2 ms collection window. Fairness is by request count; it does not allocate equal token or compute budgets. Admission and shutdown specifies the remaining caps and state transitions.
The saved loopback run used the same 128 inputs, 16 clients and CPU work for both load variants. Batch size one made 128 backend calls; batch size eight made 16. Timings this small vary between runs, and a rerun of evaluate can reverse their order; the call counts do not change. Client errors and all attempted-request denominators remain in the JSON.
Controlled latch-backend runs also expose queued cancellation and a fifteen-request A, B, C service rotation. The saturation notes retain timings, latency quantiles, fairness scope and environment details.
Use Go 1.23 or later. The recorded race run used Go 1.25.1 and executed 26 top-level tests with zero skips. The race detector needs a working C compiler. The module uses the standard library and downloads no backend model.
gateway/ holds admission, queues, batching, the breaker, HTTP handling and their race tests.
experiment/ runs the loopback and controlled-backlog workloads.
cmd/servegate/ exposes serve, demo and evaluate.
loadtests/request.json is the small HTTP request above; benchmarks/ keeps recorded runs.
Request path and race checks connect the implementation to its invariants.
python hack/check_gateway.py --require-lint --wheel --go /path/to/real/go performs the full local verification. For this Go module, --wheel checks a built binary from a separate directory. Distributing the gateway describes that binary and its source checks.

speculative-decoding.title: Speculative Decoding
speculative-decoding.text:
Exact speculative decoding with KV-cache rollback, checked against target distributions that can be enumerated exactly. The cached block engine runs local GPT-2 and Llama checkpoints through Hugging Face Transformers. The only timing recorded so far is on tiny random CPU checkpoints, not trained models.
A draft model proposes tokens from q. The target model supplies p. For a proposed token x, the sampler accepts with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); after rejection it samples from normalized max(p-q, 0). If a whole block is accepted, it draws one extra target token.
That correction matters: accepting every plausible draft token changes the output law. This repository keeps a slow full-prefix implementation, an independently enumerated finite target law, and a cached block engine so the probability and cache rules can be checked separately.
Python 3.11+ is sufficient for these experiments. The first command checks twelve categorical cases and one history-dependent joint case. joint enumerates every positive-probability path for a bounded target horizon, including variable-length stop leaves, then compares samples path by path. It reports target mass, counts, total variation, illegal outputs, and a simultaneous Hoeffding reference band. Finite-sample agreement is evidence, not a proof for arbitrary models. Enumeration is limited to eight output tokens and an explicit leaf budget.
The cached implementation supports unpadded batch-one GPT-2 and standard-RoPE Llama with DynamicCache, eager attention, and unquantized weights. It retains only the required final k+1 logit rows. A rejected branch crops both cache state and its token ledger; a forward failure resets them before reuse. Sliding/static caches, nonstandard RoPE, quantization, and multi-request batching are outside this implementation.
The stored random-checkpoint run used a 31,616-parameter target, a 6,384-parameter draft, CPU float32, and one torch thread:
Each measured request started with empty caches and included prefill; loading and warmups were excluded. The checkpoints were generated locally and deleted after the run. This is one fixed-order CPU fixture measurement, not a trained-model or GPU speedup result. The measurement record retains physical forward/input-token counters, stopping differences, and all setup details.
To repeat that fixture after installing .[hf], run python bench/time_random_checkpoints.py --output artifacts/tiny-cpu.json. To use existing local weights:
Token-to-ID mappings, special tokens, vocabulary support, and context limits must agree. The loader does not download checkpoints or enable remote code. More accepted tokens do not necessarily mean less total token work; inspect physical forwards, cache crops, and input-token counts alongside elapsed time.
Run RUN_ML_SMOKE=1 PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s checks -v with the HF extra to include local random GPT-2/Llama tests. Without the extra, optional tests skip explicitly. python bench/check_sampling.py --require-lint --wheel also checks the installed wheel. See the correctness notebook, measurement protocol, and check record. Historical mutation traces retain the paths used when they were recorded.

temporal-rag.title: Temporal RAG
temporal-rag.text:
RAG over facts that change returns the right sentence from the wrong point in time.
Recovered 19/19 exact source sets vs 11/19 for a lexical + recency baseline (synthetic facts).
Who owned Atlas on February 15? The answer can change when the question is asked with a later knowledge cutoff:
The correction does not rewrite the older knowledge snapshot. This retriever separates when a fact applies, when it was recorded, and which committed corpus revision a reader sees. Conflicting active facts at the latest valid boundary produce an abstention with provenance.
Python 3.11+ and SQLite 3.35+ support the persistent path. Use a fresh database for the import example:
Appends are immutable and compare the caller's expected commit version under the writer transaction. A stale version fails before insertion. A read snapshot can stay pinned while another connection commits a correction. Existing event IDs cannot be overwritten or deleted through the store.
The small fixture contains 13 events and 19 independently labeled cases. Timestamp-aware retrieval recovered the exact source set in 19/19 cases; a lexical-plus-recency baseline recovered 11/19. Those are structured synthetic facts scored with a deterministic answerer.
The larger storage experiment compared 128 indexed queries over 11,497 events with an independent Python scan and found zero source-ID mismatches. The report includes actual query plans, VM-step estimates, append work and local timings. It avoids scanning unrelated fact keys; it still processes the eligible history for the requested key.
The optional hf-evaluate command accepts an existing local safetensors checkpoint and validates generated JSON against retrieved evidence. Its recorded status is not run, with zero generation calls. The reference results do not measure generated-answer quality.
Both time cutoffs are inclusive, timezone aware UTC microseconds. A correction must target the same entity, attribute and effective boundary at a strictly later recording time. Divergent visible corrections remain conflicting evidence rather than being settled by recording recency.
Structured metadata is application-owned. Retrieved document text cannot change these rules or grant capabilities. Citation checks establish support in the supplied context, not external truth or the completeness of that context. Availability timestamps are supplied provenance. Long-held WAL readers can retain pages; the store has no retention service, source authentication or tenant ACL layer.
Start with the bitemporal layout, then the indexed algorithm. Query reference contains the complete API, generation budgets and import limits.
The recorded suite has 58 tests. Reproduction notes link the software-check artifact; sharing the event log describes what belongs in a release.

tool-calling-lab.title: Tool Calling Lab
tool-calling-lab.text:
A tool call can parse and still be wrong: missing item, illegal route, dropped action.

Compiling the sentence is only the first check. The item must exist at the destination, the route must stay inside the grid, and a response must preserve the requested actions. This repository keeps those checks separate from model generation, then uses them to create supervised and preference-training data.
Python 3.11 or later is enough for the simulator and reference experiment:
The first command scores a handwritten controlled-language compiler. Its 36/36 reference result checks the dataset and executor, not learned accuracy. A JSON-valid program can still fail execution; a program that ends in the correct position can still omit a required pickup. Reports retain all of those distinctions.
The robot has move, pick, and drop tools on a 7 by 7 grid. Responses allow at most eight calls and one to three cells per movement. The executor checks intermediate cells and returns a new state only after the whole program succeeds. It exposes no shell or filesystem tools.
The optional ml extra provides completion-only LoRA SFT and a directly implemented DPO objective. Supply a local causal-model checkpoint:
DPO pairs receive rewards from independent state labels and canonical action traces. The policy and frozen reference score completion tokens, including EOS, with prompt/padding tokens masked. Adapter, optimizer, RNG and data/configuration identities are committed together. Increasing the requested total steps can resume a run; changing its training data or objective settings cannot.
The controlled-language task families are held out by composition:
Phrases and item vocabularies also differ by split. The reference compiler knows all families. These partitions test specified compositions rather than unrestricted language understanding.
Preference optimization gives the likelihood equations and checkpoint protocol. Robot execution defines the action boundary. The longer command reference covers base/adapter comparison and token limits.
The two-step DPO run's held-out execution result was 0/2; its record is kept unchanged. No pretrained adaptation gain or GPU performance result has been measured.
Use checks and reproduction to interpret skipped versus executed tests, and sharing checkpoints when preparing an archive or GitHub release.
